correctness.rationale: For m=min_i x_i, the product lies between m^n and m, and m-m^n has maximum h_n at t_n; the diagonal attains it. The clipped shift of m by h_n/2 has error at most h_n/2 on the whole cube, hence in all models, and rational shifts approach it uniformly. On a singleton unit loop both modalities are identities and each extended term is 1-Lipschitz in the sup norm. The two diagonal valuations at t_n and 1 force error at least (t_n-t_n^n)/2; saturation forces endpoint values t_n-e_n and 1-e_n and the slope-one segment between them. At rational input 1 a rational term has rational output, but e_n=(n-1)t_n/(2n) is irrational for n>=3 by the monic rational-root theorem and 2^(n-1)>n. For n=2 the shift 1/8 works, and t_n tends to 1 so e_n tends to 1/2. In the plain language the diagonal branch on (1/2,1) is one of 0, 1-s, s, 1, by fixed order and closure; any improvement needs value 1 at s=1 and thus branch s or 1. These incur at least h_n at t_n (by continuity for n=2) or 1-2^(-n)>h_n at 1/2, respectively.
residual_risks: The grid checker is corroboration only; the all-model and irrationality assertions are justified analytically, not by a grid or floating-point error comparison.

value.rationale: The product is a standard alternative conjunction. Quantifying its distance from the weaker languages and identifying exactly when dense rational syntax fails to contain an optimizer establish a useful expressivity boundary. The singleton saturation witness explains why greater modal depth cannot repair it; this is a substantive distinction from the available strong Łukasiewicz benchmark, even though the unrestricted metric calculation is elementary.
residual_risks: The result is specific to the stated languages and product target and does not by itself classify approximation to other t-norms or restricted model classes.
